paras: The lynching of Josh Shorter was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Eufaula, Alabama, on June 9, 1881. Shorter, accused of assaulting a young white girl the day before, was captured across the river in Georgia and hanged from a tree after a crowd kept him from the sheriff. The Savannah Morning News headlined the news "Speedy Vengeance," and a brief wire item carried it to papers as far away as Utah and California.

According to a Eufaula dispatch printed in the Savannah Morning News, Shorter was accused of "a most villainous outrage" on "a respectable white girl, twelve years old" near the city late on the afternoon of June 8. A second Eufaula dispatch, in the Alexandria Gazette, described him as "a negro boy, aged sixteen years" and also gave the girl's age as twelve. The New York Sun placed the alleged assault on the evening of Wednesday, June 8, and called the girl a white school girl "18 years old."

A "diligent pursuit by a large party" followed, and Shorter was captured across the river in Georgia on the morning of June 9. His captors brought him back to the Alabama side, where the sheriff attempted to take possession of him. Instead, "a large crowd" hurried him back to the Georgia side and hanged him from a limb of a large tree about midway between Eufaula and Georgetown.
The Sun reported that the body was still hanging at nightfall. A Montgomery wire item said only that the accused man was caught on the Georgia side of the river and "hanged by a mob."
No report of an inquest, arrest, or prosecution of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named the girl or any member of the crowd.

The Savannah Morning News ran the fullest account on its front page on June 10 under the headlines "Speedy Vengeance" and "A White Girl Attacked by a Negro Near Eufaula--The Fiend Caught and Lynched." The Alexandria Gazette printed a separate Eufaula dispatch the same day under "Lynching a Negro," stating the assault as fact.

Northern and western papers carried the story mainly as a one-sentence wire item among other crime news. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and a Daily Republican wire column described the victim only as "a colored man, accused of feloniously assaulting a little girl," printing it beside a triple lynching in Sevier County, Arkansas. The Montgomery version, which said the man "grossly assaulted" the girl, ran in the Salt Lake Herald and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on June 11, the latter under the head "Swift Punishment," and reached the Washington Standard by June 17. The New York Sun's brief of June 13, headed "A Negro Lynched," named Shorter and described the pursuit, capture, and hanging without comment.

The two Eufaula dispatches gave the girl's age as twelve, while the Sun's later summary gave eighteen. The Savannah dispatch placed the hanging on the Georgia side of the river, whereas the Alexandria dispatch said Shorter was "lynched here," at Eufaula.

accounts.label: Eufaula dispatch (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: Shorter was captured in Georgia, brought to the Alabama side, and, when the sheriff tried to take him, hurried back to Georgia by a large crowd and hanged from a tree midway between Eufaula and Georgetown.

accounts.label: Eufaula dispatch (Alexandria Gazette)
accounts.gist: Shorter, a sixteen-year-old 'negro boy', was 'lynched here yesterday' for an assault on a twelve-year-old white girl.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire
accounts.gist: An unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a little girl near Eufaula was caught on the Georgia side of the river and hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: New York Sun summary
accounts.gist: A white school girl, '18 years old', was assaulted on the evening of June 8; Shorter was pursued, captured, and hanged from a tree limb, still hanging at nightfall.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the Eufaula dispatch 'SPEEDY VENGEANCE' and 'The Fiend Caught and Lynched', calling the alleged assault 'a most villainous outrage'.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran the Montgomery wire under 'Swift Punishment', with the assault stated as fact.
The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and Daily Republican printed the wire item, which says 'accused of', among other crime briefs.
The Alexandria Gazette ('Lynching a Negro') and New York Sun ('A Negro Lynched') reported without comment but stated the assault as fact.

conflicts.note: The two Eufaula dispatches agree on twelve; the Sun's '18' is a later New York summary and may be a misprint.
